title: Stand firm
hook: the good lies in the will, so stand firm there (Discourses 1.29)

segments.voice: Yesterday: a good opponent, the rough sparring partner the trainer chose. What difficulty did you meet as training? Day four hundred six, the end of the week.

A tree in a storm doesn't stay still. The branches thrash, leaves tear off, the whole crown bends sideways. What keeps it standing is underneath, where you can't see: the roots, gripping the ground. A tree that tried to hold every leaf in place would snap. Epictetus has a whole chapter on constancy, on staying steady when pressure comes, and his advice runs the same way as the tree's. Know where your roots are. Today: stand firm.
screen: `A TREE IN A STORM.` → `BRANCHES THRASH, ROOTS HOLD.` → `KNOW WHERE YOUR ROOTS ARE.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty-nine, on constancy. It opens with a short, dense claim. The good, Epictetus says, is a certain state of the will. So is the bad. And everything outside the will, money, health, reputation, even the body, is material the will works with. Earlier in the Discourses he puts it this way: as wood is the carpenter's material, each person's own life is the material of the art of living. The carpenter isn't good because the wood is fine; he's good because of what he does with it. That's where the roots are. If your good lives in your will, then pressure on everything else is weather in the branches. A threat to your job, your comfort, your standing: those are leaves. Real things, worth caring about, but not the roots. Epictetus then imagines the test. Someone powerful threatens you. Don't panic, he says; ask what is being threatened. If it's the body or the property, the will is still standing. He even pictures God calling a student forward as a witness: come and testify for me. Is anything outside the will good or bad? Will you show up and say it, or will you tremble and say the opposite? Constancy isn't stiffness. It isn't refusing to feel the wind. It's knowing which part of you is supposed to move and which part isn't. Look back at the week: never alone, blind, not wicked, a clay lamp, not my judgment, test the coin, a good opponent. And today, stand firm.
screen: `THE GOOD IS A STATE OF THE WILL.` · `EVERYTHING ELSE IS MATERIAL.` · `CALLED FORWARD AS A WITNESS.` · `NOT STIFFNESS: KNOWING THE ROOTS.` · then, large: `STAND FIRM.`

segments.voice: Sit with your feet flat on the floor. Feel the ground under you, solid. Breathe. Now bring to mind one pressure you're under: a deadline, a hard conversation, someone's expectations. Let it blow through you like wind. Notice what bends: plans, comfort, mood. Then come back to your feet on the floor, and to what doesn't need to bend: what you value, how you intend to act. Stay there, rooted. The bell holds the time.
Stand firm. Epictetus' constancy: the good lives in the will, so let the branches move in the wind and keep the roots where they are.
Your line: stand firm. When pressure comes today, let what can bend, bend, and stay steady in the one place that's yours. Day four hundred six, and a week done.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners prepare for pressure by naming in advance what could be lost and what couldn't, and anchoring themselves in their own choices.

original.note: Greek eustatheia: steadiness, standing well; the title word of Discourses 1.29.

trapdoor: what you thought: be tough, don't bend.
what it means: let the outside things move; stay rooted in the will, where the good is.
what a scholar hears: 1.29 opens with the claim that the essence of the good is a certain kind of prohairesis, and of the bad likewise; everything else is material.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.15 (wood as the carpenter's material, life as the material of the art of living)

notes: Discourses 1.29 paraphrased: the essence of good as a certain will; externals as materials (Epictetus uses analogies of a craftsman's materials; check whether carpenter/wood is his example or the script's); the threatened student; the witness called by God. Confirm.
Tree-and-roots image is the script's own, not Epictetus'.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the carpenter/wood analogy was attributed to 1.29 (and a doctor/patient pair added); the wood image is from 1.15, now credited as 'earlier in the Discourses' and added to sources; the witness now gives God's actual question in 1.29 ('is anything outside the will good or bad?'); 'his secret', trapdoor 'as plainly as anywhere' and howItsDone 'often' softened.
